blocks.html: In Halves of the World you met two famous lines: the equator, around the middle of Earth, and the prime meridian, from the North Pole to the South Pole. Mapmakers draw many more lines like them. Together they make a net, or grid, that covers the whole globe.
Parallels (lines of latitude) are circles that run east and west around the globe. Meridians (lines of longitude) are half circles that run north and south, from pole to pole.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: Drag the globe. The gray grid shows parallels (around) and meridians (pole to pole).

blocks.html: Parallels are called that because they never meet: like the rails of a train track, they stay the same distance apart all the way around. Meridians all meet at the North Pole and the South Pole, like the lines between the sections of an orange. So they are far apart at the equator and squeeze together near the poles.

head: Parallels (latitude)
Meridians (longitude)
blocks.cap: The two kinds of lines side by side.

blocks.title: Which line is which?
blocks.q: A line runs from the North Pole straight down to the South Pole. Is it a parallel or a meridian? What does it help you measure?
steps: It runs north and south, from pole to pole.
Lines from pole to pole are meridians.
Meridians are used to measure how far east or west a place is.
blocks.a: A meridian. It measures east-west position (longitude).

blocks.title: The tricky part
blocks.q: Parallels run east and west. So do they measure how far east you are?
steps: Walk along one parallel: you go east or west, but your distance from the equator stays the same.
Step from one parallel to the next: now you have moved north or south.
So the parallel you are on tells how far north or south you are.
blocks.a: No. Parallels measure north-south position (latitude), even though they run east-west.

blocks.html: Many people mix the two up because of the directions. Parallels run east-west but measure north-south; meridians run north-south but measure east-west. A check that works: latitude lines lie flat, like the rungs of a ladder (a "ladder-tude"), and you climb a ladder up and down, north and south.

blocks.cap: Half the world on a flat map, with the grid every 30 degrees. Parallels are the flat lines; meridians are the up-and-down lines.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: You now know that parallels circle the globe east and west. Each parallel has a number, its latitude, measured in degrees (°).
Latitude tells how many degrees north or south of the equator a place is. The equator is 0°. The North Pole is 90° N and the South Pole is 90° S. Every latitude needs its letter: N or S.

Imagine a line from the center of Earth to the equator and another to your town. The angle between them is your latitude. Go all the way to a pole and the angle is a right angle, 90°. You cannot go farther north than the North Pole, so no latitude is more than 90°.

blocks.name: gg-latlon
blocks.cap: Drag the pin (or use the arrow keys) to 45° N. Watch the readout: only the up-and-down position changes the latitude.

blocks.title: Reading a latitude
blocks.q: A town is on the parallel halfway between the equator and the North Pole. What is its latitude?
steps: The equator is 0° and the North Pole is 90° N.
Halfway between 0 and 90 is 45.
The town is north of the equator, so the letter is N.

blocks.title: Same number, two places
blocks.q: Two cities are both 34° from the equator. One is Los Angeles, the other is Sydney, Australia. How do we write each latitude?
steps: Los Angeles is north of the equator: 34° N.
Sydney is south of the equator: 34° S.
Both are the same distance from the equator, on opposite sides.
blocks.a: Los Angeles about 34° N; Sydney about 34° S.

blocks.html: Writing "latitude 40°" without a letter. There are two parallels at 40°, one north and one south of the equator, so "40°" could be in Spain or in New Zealand. Always add N or S. And if you ever get a latitude above 90°, something is wrong: check whether you meant longitude.

blocks.cap: The Southern Hemisphere is shaded. Every place there has a latitude marked S.

blocks.html: Latitude alone cannot pin down a place: lots of towns share one parallel. We also need to know how far east or west a place is. That is the job of the meridians.

Longitude tells how many degrees east or west of the prime meridian a place is. The prime meridian, 0°, runs through Greenwich, in London, England. Longitude goes up to 180° E and 180° W, which meet on the far side of the globe.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The prime meridian (0°) runs from pole to pole through Greenwich. Drag the globe to the far side to find 180°.

blocks.html: Unlike the equator, the prime meridian is not set by nature. Any meridian could have been 0°. In 1884, at a meeting in Washington, D.C., delegates from 25 countries chose the one through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, mainly because most of the world's ships already used sea charts based on it. From there you count 180° east and 180° west, which makes 360°, a full circle.

blocks.title: Counting west
blocks.q: A meridian is 75° west of the prime meridian. How do you write its longitude? Which continent does it cross north of the equator?
steps: Count west from 0° at Greenwich.
75° west is written 75° W.
Going 75° west from London crosses the Atlantic and reaches eastern North America (it passes near Philadelphia).

blocks.title: Across the globe
blocks.q: What longitude is exactly on the other side of the globe from the prime meridian?
steps: Half a circle is 360° ÷ 2 = 180°.
Going 180° east or 180° west lands on the same meridian.
So it is written just 180°, with no letter.

blocks.html: Thinking longitude goes up to 360°, or that the prime meridian runs all the way around Earth like the equator. The prime meridian is only a half circle, pole to pole. Its other half, on the opposite side of the globe, is the 180° meridian. So longitudes run 0° to 180° E and 0° to 180° W, and every one needs its letter, E or W.

blocks.name: gg-latlon
blocks.cap: Drag the pin to 75° W. Only the left-right position changes the longitude.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: Put latitude and longitude together and you get a place's coordinates: an address that works anywhere on Earth, even in the middle of the ocean.
Write latitude first, then longitude, each with its letter: Washington, D.C., is at about 39° N, 77° W.

blocks.name: gg-latlon
blocks.cap: Washington, D.C., on a grid every 10 degrees: up from the equator to 39° N, left of the prime meridian to 77° W.

blocks.html: Geographers and sailors wrote latitude first long before graphs were invented, because latitude was the easier one to find: you can measure it from the height of the Sun at noon or the North Star at night. Longitude needed accurate clocks, which came much later. The habit stuck, so every map, atlas and GPS writes latitude first.

blocks.title: Reading a point
blocks.q: A point sits on the parallel marked 30° S and on the meridian marked 60° W. Write its coordinates.
steps: Latitude first: the parallel is 30° S.
Then longitude: the meridian is 60° W.
Put them together with a comma.

blocks.title: Between the lines
blocks.q: On a map with lines every 10°, a dot is halfway between 40° N and 50° N, and exactly on 10° E. Where is it?
steps: Halfway between 40 and 50 is 45, so the latitude is 45° N.
The longitude is on the line: 10° E.
Latitude first.

blocks.html: Writing the longitude first, as in an (x, y) graph, or dropping the letters. "77, 39" could mean a dozen places. Check two things every time: is the first number the north-south one, and does each number have N, S, E or W? Latitude letters are N or S; longitude letters are E or W, so "39° W, 77° N" is a sure sign the order is backward.

blocks.html: Now turn it around: someone gives you coordinates, and you find the place. This is how ships, planes and rescuers find a spot on a map. You will use what you learned in Reading Coordinates.

Find the latitude first (go up for N, down for S from the equator), then move along that parallel to the longitude (right for E, left for W of the prime meridian). The place is where the two lines cross.

blocks.title: Find 35° N, 140° E
blocks.q: Which big city is at about 35° N, 140° E?
steps: Start at the equator and go up (north) to 35° N, a little past the 30° line.
Move right (east) from the prime meridian to 140° E, far into Asia.
The lines cross on the island of Honshu, in Japan.

blocks.name: gg-latlon
blocks.cap: Four cities, lettered. Which letter is at about 35° N, 140° E? (It is the one in eastern Asia.)

blocks.html: On almost every world map, north is at the top and east is on the right. So north latitudes grow upward from the equator and south latitudes grow downward; east longitudes grow to the right of the prime meridian and west longitudes grow to the left. Knowing which way the numbers grow is the whole trick.

blocks.title: A southern city
blocks.q: Which city is at about 23° S, 43° W: Rio de Janeiro, Cairo or New York?
steps: 23° S is below the equator, so the city is in the Southern Hemisphere.
43° W is left of the prime meridian: the Americas or the Atlantic.
Of the three, only Rio de Janeiro is south of the equator and in the Americas.

blocks.html: Counting the wrong way from 0°. West longitudes get bigger as you go left on the map, and south latitudes get bigger as you go down. A quick check: a place at 23° S, 43° W must be below the equator and left of the prime meridian. If your finger ends up in Africa or Asia, a letter was read backward.

blocks.cap: Practice: drag the pin to 23° S, 43° W, then press Check.

blocks.html: Besides the equator, four parallels have names. They come from the way Earth leans as it goes around the Sun. Each one has a fixed latitude.

blocks.html: The tropics are the band between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. The polar regions lie beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles.

Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4° from straight up. As Earth goes around the Sun, the spot where the noon Sun is straight overhead slides north to 23.4° N and back south to 23.4° S. Those two limits are the tropics. The polar circles are 23.4° from the poles (90 − 23.4 = 66.6), because the same tilt keeps the area inside them in all-day light or all-day dark for part of the year.

blocks.title: Which zone?
blocks.q: Bangkok, Thailand, is at about 14° N. Is it in the tropics?
steps: The tropics run from 23.4° S to 23.4° N.
14° N is between 0° and 23.4° N.
So Bangkok is inside the tropics.
blocks.a: Yes. At some point every year the noon Sun is straight overhead in Bangkok.

blocks.html: Mixing up Cancer and Capricorn. A memory trick: Cancer comes first in the alphabet, and on a map you read from the top, so Cancer is the upper, northern one. Another mistake is thinking the tropics are always the hottest places. The hottest temperatures are often in deserts near 25° to 30°, and high mountains in the tropics are cool.

blocks.html: In Halves of the World you split the world in half two ways. Now the letters in a place's coordinates tell you exactly which halves it is in.
N or S in the latitude gives the Northern or Southern Hemisphere. E or W in the longitude gives the Eastern or Western Hemisphere. Every place (not on the lines themselves) is in one of each.

blocks.title: Sydney
blocks.q: Sydney, Australia, is at about 34° S, 151° E. Which hemispheres is it in?
steps: The latitude letter is S: Southern Hemisphere.
The longitude letter is E: Eastern Hemisphere.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The Western Hemisphere shaded. Turn the globe: it includes a slice of Europe and Africa.

blocks.html: The Eastern and Western Hemispheres are split by the prime meridian (0°) and the 180° meridian. The prime meridian runs through London and western Africa, not along the edge of the Atlantic. So everything west of Greenwich, including Portugal, Ireland, most of Spain and much of West Africa, is in the Western Hemisphere.

blocks.title: A surprise
blocks.q: Dakar, Senegal, in Africa, is at about 15° N, 17° W. Which hemispheres?
steps: Latitude 15° N: Northern Hemisphere.
Longitude 17° W: Western Hemisphere, even though Dakar is in Africa.

head: Hemispheres
Letters
Example

blocks.html: Thinking the Western Hemisphere means "the Americas" and the Eastern means "Asia." Use the letters, not the continent: Lisbon (39° N, 9° W) and Accra, Ghana (6° N, 0.2° W) have W longitudes, so they are in the Western Hemisphere. And eastern Russia and some Pacific islands reach past 180°, into the Western Hemisphere.

blocks.html: A degree is a big step: about 111 km of latitude. To give a place more exactly, we split each degree into smaller parts, the same way an hour is split into minutes. You will use what you know about fractions and decimals.
One degree has 60 minutes (written ′), and one minute has 60 seconds (″). So 40° 30′ means 40 and 30/60 degrees, which is 40.5°.

Babylonian astronomers counted in sixties more than 3,000 years ago, and we still split circles and hours their way. Because 60 can be divided evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, many fractions of a degree come out as whole minutes: a quarter degree is 15′, a third is 20′.

blocks.title: Minutes to a decimal
blocks.q: Write 51° 30′ N as a decimal.
steps: 30′ is 30/60 of a degree.

blocks.title: A decimal to minutes
blocks.q: Write 33.75° S in degrees and minutes.
steps: Keep the whole degrees: 33°.
Multiply the decimal part by 60: 0.75 × 60 = 45.
So it is 33° 45′.

blocks.title: GPS signs
blocks.q: A phone shows a place at -22.9, -43.2. What does that mean?
steps: GPS apps often write south latitudes and west longitudes as negative numbers.
The first number is the latitude: -22.9 means 22.9° S.
The second is the longitude: -43.2 means 43.2° W.

blocks.html: Reading 40° 30′ as 40.30°. Minutes are sixtieths, not hundredths: 30′ is half a degree, so 40° 30′ = 40.5°. Check: the decimal part can never reach 1, and a decimal part of .30 would be only 18′. Also check the sign on GPS numbers: a minus sign means S or W.

blocks.html: How far is one degree on the ground? The answer depends on which way you go. You will use degrees and minutes and multiplication.

One degree of latitude is about 111 km (69 miles) everywhere. One degree of longitude is about 111 km at the equator but shrinks toward the poles: about 85 km at 40°, 56 km at 60°, and 0 at the poles.

Earth is about 40,000 km around. A full circle is 360°, so one degree of latitude is about 40,000 ÷ 360 ≈ 111 km. Parallels are all the same distance apart, so this works everywhere. But meridians meet at the poles. The circle of a parallel gets smaller as you go north, and the same 1° of longitude covers a shorter and shorter piece of it. (The size of that circle is the equator's size times the cosine of the latitude: half as big at 60°.)

blocks.cap: Look at the gray meridians: wide apart at the equator, crowded near the North Pole.

blocks.title: North to south
blocks.q: Two towns are on the same meridian, at 32° N and 37° N. About how far apart are they?
steps: They differ by 37 − 32 = 5 degrees of latitude.
Each degree of latitude is about 111 km.

blocks.title: East to west
blocks.q: Two towns are both at 60° N, 4° of longitude apart. About how far apart are they?
steps: At 60°, one degree of longitude is about 56 km (half of 111).
At the equator the same 4° would be 444 km.

blocks.title: One minute
blocks.q: About how far is one minute of latitude?
steps: A degree of latitude is about 111 km and has 60 minutes.
That is one nautical mile, the unit sailors and pilots use.

blocks.html: Using 111 km for every degree of longitude. That is true only at the equator. Before you multiply, ask which way you are going. North-south: 111 km per degree. East-west: smaller, unless you are near the equator. (The U.S. Geological Survey gives about 54.6 miles, or 88 km, for a degree of longitude at 38° N.)

blocks.html: In Globe or Flat Map? you saw that a globe is the truest picture of Earth, but a flat map is easier to carry and shows the whole world at once. Now let us see what the flat map gives up.

You cannot flatten a ball without stretching or tearing it. So every flat world map distorts something: sizes (areas), shapes, distances or directions. A map projection is a mapmaker's method for moving the grid of the globe onto flat paper, and each one chooses what to keep true.

Try it with an orange. Peel it and press the peel flat: it splits, or you have to squash and stretch it. Earth's surface is curved in every direction at once, so no flat sheet can match it everywhere. The mathematician Leonhard Euler proved in 1775 that no flat map can keep every distance true. A flat map can keep areas true, or keep shapes true in small areas, but not both.

blocks.name: gg-projection
blocks.cap: The same world on two projections. Greenland (and Africa) are highlighted: compare their sizes on each map.

What it means
Example

blocks.cap: Three kinds of choices. The next topics look at each.

blocks.title: Where is the stretch?
blocks.q: On the left map above, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. On the right map it looks much smaller. Which map is lying?
steps: Both maps show the same countries; only the projection differs.
Greenland is far from the equator, where the left map (Mercator) stretches things most.
The right map (Equal Earth) keeps areas true, so its sizes can be compared.
blocks.a: The left map exaggerates Greenland. On the globe, Africa is about 14 times larger.

blocks.html: Thinking one flat map is the "correct" one and the others are wrong. Every projection is a trade-off. Ask what a map is for, then pick the projection that keeps the right thing true. And when sizes matter, compare on a globe or an equal-area map.

blocks.cap: On the globe there is no stretching: compare Greenland and Africa here.

blocks.html: The most famous world map is the one Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish mapmaker, published in 1569. It was made for sailors, and it still shows up on classroom walls and web maps. You learned in Why Flat Maps Stretch that every flat map stretches something. Here is what Mercator stretches.

A Mercator map keeps angles and directions true, so small areas have the right shape and a straight line is a steady compass course. To do that, it stretches places more and more toward the poles: areas far from the equator look much too big.

blocks.name: gg-projection
blocks.cap: Drag Greenland's true-size outline toward the equator and watch it shrink.

blocks.html: On a globe, meridians come together at the poles. Mercator draws them as straight, parallel lines instead, so lands near the poles are stretched east-west. To keep shapes from looking squashed, Mercator also spreads the parallels farther apart toward the poles, stretching lands north-south by the same amount. Shapes stay right, but sizes grow: at 60° N, lengths are doubled and areas look four times too big. The poles themselves would be infinitely far away, so Mercator maps stop before them.

head: Latitude
Areas look bigger by about
blocks.cap: How much a Mercator map enlarges areas.

blocks.title: Greenland and Africa
blocks.q: On a Mercator map, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. Greenland covers about 2.17 million km² and Africa about 30.3 million km². How many times bigger is Africa?
steps: That is about 14.
Greenland looks huge because it is far north, where Mercator enlarges areas many times.

blocks.title: Why sailors liked it
blocks.q: A captain draws a straight line on a Mercator chart from Lisbon to a port in Brazil. What does the line tell her?
steps: On a Mercator map, angles are true.
So a straight line crosses every meridian at the same angle.
She can hold one compass heading the whole way.
blocks.a: The one compass direction to steer for the whole trip.

blocks.html: Believing Greenland is as big as Africa, or that Europe and North America are bigger than they are, because a Mercator map shows them that way. Check sizes on a globe or an equal-area map. Remember the rule: on Mercator, the farther from the equator, the bigger things look.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: If Mercator makes northern lands too big, can a map show every place at its true size? Yes, but it pays a price.
An equal-area map shows every country at its true size compared with every other. To do it, it bends shapes, especially near the edges and the poles. Examples: Gall-Peters, Mollweide and Equal Earth.

blocks.name: gg-projection
blocks.cap: Two equal-area maps. Greenland and Africa are in their true proportion on both, but their shapes differ.

blocks.html: Area is width times height. Near the poles, an equal-area map must squeeze lands north-south as much as it stretches them east-west, so each patch keeps its true area. Squeezing in one direction and stretching in the other changes shapes. Gall-Peters makes lands near the equator look tall and thin, and lands near the poles short and wide. Mollweide and Equal Earth curve the meridians in, which keeps shapes more natural in the middle but bends them near the edges.

blocks.title: Comparing sizes
blocks.q: You want a map showing how much of the world is covered by forest in each country. Which kind of projection should you use?
steps: You will compare amounts of land, so sizes must be fair.
An equal-area map keeps every area in true proportion.
Mercator would make northern forests look far bigger than tropical ones.
blocks.a: An equal-area map, such as Equal Earth.

blocks.title: Reading sizes
blocks.q: On an equal-area map, Brazil covers about 3 times as much map as Argentina. What does that tell you?
steps: On an equal-area map, map area is in proportion to real area.
So Brazil is about 3 times as big as Argentina in real life.
blocks.a: Brazil really is about 3 times the size of Argentina (about 8.5 million km² against 2.8 million km²).

blocks.html: Thinking an equal-area map has no distortion. It keeps one thing, area, and gives up shape. Look at Africa on Gall-Peters: it is the right size, but it looks too tall and thin. No flat map is free of distortion.

sources.name: CIA World Factbook, Geography sections of the country pages (cia.gov)

blocks.html: Mercator keeps shapes, and equal-area maps keep sizes. A third family keeps neither exactly, on purpose.

A compromise projection, such as Robinson or Winkel tripel, keeps nothing perfectly but stretches sizes, shapes and distances only a little. The whole world looks much like it does on a globe, which is why many atlases and wall maps use them.

blocks.name: gg-projection
blocks.cap: Switch between four projections and compare Greenland, Africa and Antarctica.

blocks.html: Errors in area and errors in shape trade against each other. Mercator pushes area error to the extreme to get perfect shapes; Gall-Peters does the opposite. A compromise spreads small errors over both. Arthur Robinson designed his projection in 1963 for the atlas maker Rand McNally by adjusting it until it looked right. The National Geographic Society used it for its world maps from 1988 and switched to the Winkel tripel in 1998, because Winkel's errors in area, shape and distance are smaller overall.

Best choice
Why

A world wall map for a classroom

A street map of a city

blocks.cap: Pick the map for the job.

blocks.title: Choosing a map
blocks.q: A teacher wants one world map on the wall so students get a fair picture of the whole Earth. Which projection should she choose?
steps: She is not steering a ship, so Mercator's true directions do not matter.
She wants sizes and shapes both close to the globe.
A compromise projection does that.
blocks.a: A compromise projection, such as Winkel tripel or Robinson.

blocks.html: Asking which map is "right." There is no single right map: there is a right map for a job. For navigation use Mercator, for comparing sizes an equal-area map, for a general picture of the world a compromise.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: Looking at country shapes is a hard way to judge a map, because few of us know the true shapes well. Mapmakers have a better test, invented by the French mathematician Nicolas Auguste Tissot in papers from 1859 to 1871. It uses circles. You already know the projections from Compromise Maps.

Draw same-size circles all over the globe, then project them. Where the circles get bigger, the map enlarges areas. Where they turn into ovals, it bends shapes. Circles that stay round and the same size mean no distortion there.

blocks.name: gg-projection
blocks.cap: Every circle is the same size on the globe. Switch projections and see how each map changes them.

blocks.html: A tiny circle on the globe is the simplest test shape: it has the same width in every direction. If a projection stretches more in one direction than another, the circle becomes an oval; if it stretches equally in all directions, the circle stays round but changes size. So the circles show both kinds of distortion at once.

head: What the circles do
What the map keeps
Example
rows: Stay round, but grow toward the poles
Become ovals, but keep the same area
Change a little in size and shape
blocks.cap: Reading the circles.

blocks.title: Reading a Tissot map
blocks.q: On a map, the circles near 60° N are perfectly round but about twice as wide as the circles on the equator. What kind of map is it?
steps: Round circles mean shapes are kept.
Circles twice as wide cover about four times the area, so areas are enlarged there.
Keeping shapes while enlarging areas toward the poles is what Mercator does.
blocks.a: A Mercator map (it keeps shapes; areas at 60° look 4 times too big).

blocks.title: Ovals
blocks.q: On another map, circles near the poles are squashed into wide, flat ovals, but each oval covers the same area as the circles at the equator. What does the map keep?
steps: Same area everywhere: areas are true.
Ovals: shapes are bent.

blocks.html: Judging a map by whether the countries "look right." Your idea of how countries look may come from Mercator maps. The circles are a fair test: compare their sizes to judge area, and their roundness to judge shape.

blocks.html: In How Far? The Scale Bar you used a scale bar. Big maps also give their scale as a ratio, which works like the scale drawings of math class.
A scale such as 1:100,000 means 1 unit on the map stands for 100,000 of the same unit on the ground: 1 cm on the map is 100,000 cm, or 1 km, in real life.

A ratio has no units, so it works in any unit: 1 inch on a 1:100,000 map is 100,000 inches on the ground too. The only work is changing a large number of centimeters (or inches) into kilometers (or miles). Remember: 100 cm = 1 m and 1,000 m = 1 km, so 100,000 cm = 1 km.

blocks.title: Map to ground
blocks.q: On a 1:50,000 hiking map, a trail is 6 cm long. How long is the real trail?
steps: Each cm on the map is 50,000 cm on the ground.

blocks.title: Ground to map
blocks.q: Two towns are 40 km apart. How far apart are they on a 1:1,000,000 map?
steps: On this map 1 cm stands for 1,000,000 cm = 10 km.
40 km ÷ 10 km per cm = 4 cm.

blocks.html: Not every map has the same job. Before you read a map, check its title and key to see what kind it is. This builds on Why Flat Maps Stretch and the map keys you used in Maps and Places.
Political maps show borders, countries and cities. Physical maps show landforms and water: mountains, rivers, deserts. Thematic maps show one topic, such as rainfall, population or language.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: A political map of Africa: countries in different colors, capitals as stars.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: A physical map of Africa: rivers, mountains, deserts and basins, no borders needed.

blocks.html: A map that tries to show everything becomes a mess. Each kind leaves things out so its main idea stands out. A thematic map often uses a choropleth: each area is shaded by one number, using a color scale explained in the key. It makes patterns jump out, but it gives only one value for each whole area.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: A choropleth: each country of South America shaded by its area.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: A map shows where earthquakes happened last year as red dots. What kind of map is it?
steps: It is about one topic: earthquakes.
It is not mainly about borders or landforms.

blocks.title: Reading a choropleth
blocks.q: Suppose a choropleth shades each country by its yearly rainfall, and Brazil is in the wettest class. Does every part of Brazil get that much rain?
steps: The shade stands for one number for the whole country, such as its average.
It cannot show differences inside a country.
In fact the Amazon in the north is very wet, while parts of the northeast are dry.
blocks.a: No. A choropleth gives one value per area, not what happens inside it.

blocks.html: Reading a choropleth as if it shows where things are inside each area. A country in the top class for population may have most of its people in a few cities and almost none in its deserts. For where things are inside, look for a dot map or a map of smaller areas.

blocks.html: Paper maps and coordinates are still the base of geography, but today three tools do much of the work: GPS, satellite images and GIS. They often work together, so people mix them up.

GPS finds where you are from satellite signals. Satellite images are pictures of Earth taken from space. A GIS (geographic information system) is computer software that stacks map layers to answer questions.

A GPS satellite sends out its position and the exact time. Your receiver measures how long each signal took to arrive, which gives its distance from that satellite. Distances from at least four satellites fix your latitude, longitude and height, and the time. The U.S. Space Force operates GPS and keeps at least 24 working satellites about 20,200 km up, each circling Earth twice a day. Europe (Galileo), Russia (GLONASS) and China (BeiDou) run systems like it.

Combining layers is the job of a GIS.

blocks.html: Thinking GPS is the map on your phone. GPS only gives the position, a pair of coordinates. The map, the street names and the route come from a separate map app, often built with GIS data and satellite images. GPS works with no map at all, and a map works with no GPS.

blocks.html: In U.S. Time Zones you saw that the United States has six time zones and that it gets earlier as you go west. Now we can see why, using longitude.
Earth turns all the way around, 360°, in 24 hours. So it turns 15° every hour (360 ÷ 24 = 15). Noon, when the Sun is highest, sweeps west around the world, and each time zone is about 15° wide.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: Earth turns toward the east. Places to the east see the Sun rise, reach noon and set before places to the west.

blocks.html: Before time zones, every town set its clocks by its own Sun: noon was when the Sun was highest. A town 15° east of you had noon one hour earlier than you did. That worked until trains made people travel fast; railroad timetables needed shared times. In the 1880s, railroads and then countries adopted zones, each about 15° wide, using the same clock time across the whole zone. The zones are counted from Greenwich, as hours ahead of (+) or behind (−) UTC, the time at the prime meridian.

blocks.title: Degrees to hours
blocks.q: Earth turns 15° each hour. How many hours does it take to turn 75°?
steps: Divide by 15: 75 ÷ 15 = 5.

blocks.title: Sun time
blocks.q: Town A is 45° of longitude east of Town B. When it is noon by the Sun in Town B, what is the Sun time in Town A?
steps: 45° ÷ 15° per hour = 3 hours.
Places to the east are ahead: they have already had their noon.
So Town A is 3 hours later: 3 p.m.

blocks.name: gg-timezones
blocks.cap: World time zones (standard time). Move the slider to change the time in London and watch every clock.

blocks.html: Thinking time zones follow straight lines every 15°. They roughly do over the oceans, but on land they bend around countries and states, because a country wants its towns on the same clock. China uses one time zone, UTC+8, even though it spans about 60° of longitude, from about 73° E to 135° E; at the same clock time, the Sun is much higher in the east than in the far west. India uses UTC+5:30, halfway between two whole-hour zones.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: You did time-zone math in What Time Is It There? by counting zones. Around the world it is easier to use each place's UTC offset, the number of hours it is ahead of (+) or behind (−) UTC. You will need negative numbers.
To find the time somewhere else: subtract your offset to get UTC, then add the other place's offset. In one step: add the difference of the two offsets.

head: City
Standard offset
City
Standard offset
blocks.cap: Standard-time offsets. In summer, places with daylight saving time move their clocks one hour ahead.

blocks.html: UTC is the shared reference clock. A place at UTC+9 is 9 hours ahead of it, so to get back to UTC you take 9 hours away; a place at UTC−5 is 5 hours behind, so you add 5. Once everything is in UTC, adding the second offset gives the other place's clock. Going through UTC means you never have to remember which way to count.

blocks.title: New York to Tokyo
blocks.q: It is 8:00 p.m. on Monday in New York (UTC−5). What time is it in Tokyo (UTC+9)?
steps: To UTC: 8:00 p.m. − (−5) = 8:00 p.m. + 5 hours = 1:00 a.m. Tuesday.
To Tokyo: 1:00 a.m. + 9 hours = 10:00 a.m. Tuesday.
Check: the difference is 9 − (−5) = 14 hours; 8 p.m. + 14 hours = 10 a.m. the next day.

blocks.title: A half-hour zone
blocks.q: It is 9:00 a.m. in London (UTC+0). What time is it in New Delhi (UTC+5:30)?
steps: London is on UTC, so UTC is 9:00 a.m.
Add 5 hours 30 minutes: 2:30 p.m.

blocks.name: gg-timezones
blocks.cap: At 9:00 a.m. in London: look at the clocks for New Delhi and Kathmandu.

blocks.html: Forgetting that some offsets are not whole hours (India UTC+5:30, Nepal UTC+5:45, Iran UTC+3:30) or that the answer can fall on a different day. After you add, ask: did I pass midnight? If the hour goes past 12 midnight it is the next day; if it goes back before midnight, it is the day before.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: Keep adding hours as you go east from London and you reach UTC+12; keep going west and you reach UTC−12. Those two meet on the far side of the world, near the 180° meridian. Something has to give there, and it is the date. This builds on Time Around the World.

The International Date Line runs roughly along 180° longitude. Cross it going west and you skip ahead one day. Cross it going east and you go back one day. The clock time stays about the same; only the date changes.

blocks.name: gg-globe
blocks.cap: The 180° meridian. A: Samoa (UTC+13), with American Samoa (UTC−11) just east of it. B: Auckland. C: Honolulu. D: Kiritimati, Kiribati (UTC+14). The date line bends east around Samoa and Kiritimati.

blocks.name: gg-timezones
blocks.cap: At midnight in London, it is already noon in Auckland but still 2:00 p.m. yesterday in Honolulu.

blocks.html: Travel east around the world and you set your watch ahead one hour in each zone: 24 hours in all, a whole extra day, by the time you get home. Without a date line, your calendar would be a day off. The date line fixes it: going east you set the date back one day when you cross it, and going west you set it forward. It zigzags around island countries so each one keeps a single date.

blocks.title: Crossing west
blocks.q: A ship crosses the date line sailing west at noon on Tuesday. What day is it just after it crosses?
steps: Going west across the date line, skip ahead one day.
Tuesday becomes Wednesday; the time stays noon.

blocks.title: Two neighbors, two dates
blocks.q: Samoa (UTC+13) and American Samoa (UTC−11) are islands less than 200 km apart. It is 10:00 a.m. on Saturday in Samoa. What day and time is it in American Samoa?
steps: The difference in offsets is 13 − (−11) = 24 hours.
American Samoa is 24 hours behind.
Same clock time, one day earlier.

blocks.html: Samoa switched sides of the date line in December 2011, so its clocks would match those of its trading partners, Australia and New Zealand. To do it, the country skipped Friday, December 30, 2011, going straight from Thursday to Saturday.

Getting the direction backward. Places just west of the date line, such as Kiribati (UTC+14) and Samoa, are the first to start each new day. Places just east of it, such as American Samoa (UTC−11), are among the last. Going west across the line: add a day. Going east: subtract a day. A way to remember: in the west Pacific, it is already "tomorrow."

blocks.html: In Find the Continents you found the seven continents by their shapes. Now let us compare them: how big they are, and how many people live on each.

Asia is the largest continent, by area and by number of people. Africa is second in both. Australia is the smallest continent, and Antarctica has no permanent residents, only scientists and staff who come and go.

head: Continent
Area (about, million km²)
Rank by area

blocks.html: A continent is a very large landmass, but geographers also count history and culture. That is why Europe is a continent even though it is joined to Asia: together they form one landmass, Eurasia. The usual dividing line runs down the Ural Mountains and the Ural River to the Caspian Sea, then along the Caucasus Mountains to the Black Sea. Some countries, such as Russia, Kazakhstan and Türkiye (Turkey), lie on both sides.

blocks.title: Ordering by size
blocks.q: Put these continents in order from largest to smallest: Europe, Africa, South America.
steps: Africa is about 30.3 million km².
South America is about 17.8 million km².
Europe is about 10.2 million km².

blocks.title: How many times?
blocks.q: About how many times bigger is Asia than Australia?
steps: Round to a friendly number.

blocks.html: Thinking Europe is a separate landmass with water all around it, like Australia. Europe and Asia are joined along a long land border; the line between them is a choice people made, mostly following the Ural Mountains and the Caucasus. Some books count six continents (joining Europe and Asia, or North and South America); this course uses seven.

blocks.html: You know the five oceans from The Five Oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic, from largest to smallest. Around their edges are smaller bodies of salt water called seas, gulfs and bays.
A sea is a smaller part of the ocean, partly enclosed by land. The Mediterranean, Caribbean, Arabian, South China, North, Black, Red and Bering Seas are some of the most important.

blocks.html: All the oceans are joined into one World Ocean; the names are a way to talk about its parts. A sea is named where land closes in around part of the ocean, so its water, waves and life can differ from the open ocean. The Black Sea connects to the Mediterranean through narrow straits, and the Mediterranean to the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar.

blocks.title: Which ocean?
blocks.q: A ship sails from the Red Sea into open water to the south. Which ocean is it in?
steps: The Red Sea opens at its south end into the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea.
Those are parts of the Indian Ocean.

blocks.html: Thinking a sea is the same as a lake, or that every "sea" is part of the ocean. Most seas are arms of the ocean. But the Caspian Sea and the Dead Sea are salty lakes: land surrounds them, and their water never reaches the ocean. Check the map: does the water connect to an ocean?

blocks.html: A river flows from its source to its mouth, as you learned in A River's Journey. The world's great rivers have carried people and goods for thousands of years, and many of the oldest cities grew up along them.
The great rivers to know: the Nile and Congo (Africa), the Amazon (South America), the Mississippi (North America), the Yangtze, Ganges and Mekong (Asia), and the Danube and Volga (Europe).

blocks.html: Rivers flow downhill, so the direction depends on where the high ground is, not on north and south. The Nile starts in the highlands of East Africa and flows north to the Mediterranean. Some record holders: the Amazon carries the most water, about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the oceans; the Yangtze is the longest river in Asia; the Volga is the longest in Europe; the Danube flows through or along ten countries.

blocks.title: Which way?
blocks.q: Cairo is near the Nile's mouth. Is Cairo upstream or downstream from Khartoum, Sudan, which is south of it?
steps: The Nile flows north, into the Mediterranean.
Water at Khartoum flows on north toward Cairo.
So Cairo is downstream.

blocks.html: Thinking the Nile flows south because Egypt is at the "top" of Africa and things fall "down" on a map. North is not downhill. And which river is longest? Most lists put the Nile first (about 6,650 km) with the Amazon close behind, but some studies that trace the Amazon from a farther source find it longer. The answer depends on where you say a river begins.
You met mountains in Mountains, Hills and Valleys. The world's great ranges are long chains of mountains, and their highest peaks are the roof of the world.

The Himalayas in Asia hold Mount Everest, 8,849 m, the highest mountain above sea level. The Andes in South America are the longest range on land, more than 7,000 km. Know the Rockies, Alps, Urals and Atlas Mountains too.

blocks.html: The highest ranges are young mountains where two of Earth's plates push together. The Himalayas are still rising as the plate carrying India presses into the rest of Asia, and the Andes rise where the Pacific seafloor dives under South America. Old ranges such as the Urals and the Appalachians have been worn down for hundreds of millions of years, so they are lower and rounder. (Earth & Space explains plates in detail.)

blocks.title: Comparing heights
blocks.q: How much higher is Everest than Aconcagua?

blocks.html: Thinking the highest mountains are near the poles because it is cold there. Height comes from plates pushing together, not from latitude: Everest is at about 28° N, and Kilimanjaro is only about 3° south of the equator. Cold comes from height: the higher you go, the colder it gets, so even equator peaks can have snow.
In Deserts, Forests and Grasslands you learned that a desert is a very dry place. Deserts cover about a third of Earth's land, and they are not all hot.

A desert is a place that gets very little precipitation, usually less than 250 mm (10 inches) a year. The Sahara is the largest hot desert. The Atacama is the driest place outside the poles. Antarctica is the largest desert of all.

blocks.html: Most hot deserts sit near 20° to 30° north and south of the equator. Air that rises over the equator drops its rain there, then sinks again near those latitudes as dry air, so clouds rarely form. Other deserts form in the rain shadow of mountains (the Atacama is shielded by the Andes) or deep inside continents, far from the ocean (the Gobi). Antarctica counts because almost no new snow falls there each year.

blocks.title: Hot or cold?
blocks.q: The Gobi is in Mongolia, far from any ocean. It is very dry. Is it a hot desert?
steps: It is far north (about 40° to 45° N) and far inland.
Its winters are long and freezing.
blocks.a: No. The Gobi is a cold desert.

blocks.html: Thinking a desert must be hot and sandy. A desert is defined by dryness, not heat. Antarctica and the Gobi are cold deserts, and most deserts are rock and gravel, not sand dunes.
Rivers from Great Rivers of the World fill lakes and pour over waterfalls. A few lakes and falls hold world records.

The Caspian Sea is the largest lake by area (about 371,000 km²). Lake Baikal in Russia is the deepest (1,642 m) and holds the most fresh water. Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake by area (about 82,100 km²). Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall (979 m).

blocks.html: Baikal sits in a deep crack in Earth's crust that has been widening for about 25 million years, which makes it both the deepest and the oldest lake. Superior is wide but shallower, so Baikal holds more water even though its surface is much smaller. Angel Falls pours off the edge of a flat-topped mountain called Auyán-tepui.

blocks.title: Area or depth?
blocks.q: Lake Superior covers about 82,100 km²; Lake Baikal about 31,700 km². Which holds more water?
steps: Area is only the surface.
Baikal is far deeper: 1,642 m at its deepest.
Volume depends on area and depth together.
blocks.a: Lake Baikal (about 23,600 km³, nearly twice as much as Superior).

blocks.html: Thinking the Caspian Sea is part of the ocean because of its name. Land surrounds it on every side, and its water never flows to the ocean, so geographers call it a lake, a salty one. The Dead Sea and the Great Salt Lake are salty lakes too.
An island has water all around it, and a peninsula has water on three sides, as you learned in Islands and Peninsulas. Here are the biggest ones on Earth.

Greenland is the largest island (about 2.17 million km²). Next come New Guinea, Borneo and Madagascar. Great peninsulas include the Arabian (the largest), Iberian, Scandinavian, Italian and Korean peninsulas.

blocks.html: Size alone does not decide what is a continent. Australia is about 3.5 times bigger than Greenland, but geographers count it as a continent because it sits on its own continental plate and has a long separate history. So the largest island is the largest piece of land that is not a continent: Greenland.

blocks.title: Island or peninsula?
blocks.q: Italy is joined to the rest of Europe in the north and has sea on its other three sides. Is it an island or a peninsula? What about Sicily, just off its toe?
steps: Water on three sides and joined to land on one: a peninsula.
Sicily has water all around: an island.
blocks.a: Italy is a peninsula; Sicily is an island.

blocks.html: Calling Australia the largest island. Australia is a continent, so Greenland is the largest island. Also, Greenland looks bigger than it is on many maps: it is a little bigger than Mexico, not the size of Africa.

blocks.html: In Opposite Pairs you saw that a strait is the water version of an isthmus. Straits and canals are where seas meet, and ships from all over the world squeeze through them.

A strait is a narrow passage of water joining two larger bodies of water. A canal is a waterway dug by people. Key straits: Gibraltar, the Bosporus, Hormuz, Malacca and Bering. Key canals: Panama and Suez.

blocks.html: Ships save huge distances through these passages. Before the Panama Canal, a ship from New York to San Francisco had to sail around the southern tip of South America. Before the Suez Canal, ships between Europe and Asia sailed around Africa. Because so many ships use them, straits and canals matter to trade all over the world.

blocks.q: A ship leaves the Mediterranean heading for the Atlantic. Which strait does it pass through?
steps: The Mediterranean's only natural opening to the Atlantic is at its west end.
There Spain and Morocco nearly touch.

blocks.html: Mixing up a strait and an isthmus. A strait is narrow water between two pieces of land; an isthmus is narrow land between two bodies of water. A canal is a strait made by people, and it is often dug across an isthmus, as at Panama and Suez.

Weather is what the air is doing today. Climate is the usual pattern of weather over many years: how warm, how wet, and when. You already know latitude and the equator. Latitude is the biggest climate control, but not the only one.
Six things together set a place's climate: latitude, elevation (height above sea level), nearness to the ocean, ocean currents, winds, and mountains that block rain.

Example
rows: Near the equator the Sun is high all year: warm. Near the poles it is low: cold.
Singapore is hot; Oslo is cool
Air gets colder as you go up, about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m on average.
Quito, Ecuador, almost on the equator, is mild all year at 2,850 m
Water heats and cools slowly, so coasts have milder summers and winters.

Warm currents warm the coasts they pass; cold currents cool them.
The North Atlantic Current keeps western Europe mild

blocks.html: Climate is about energy and water. Latitude sets the sunshine; thin air high up holds less heat; oceans store summer heat and give it back in winter; winds and currents carry heat and moisture; mountains make air rise, cool and drop its rain.

blocks.title: Going up
blocks.q: A town at sea level has an average temperature of 26 °C. About how warm is a mountain village 2,000 m higher nearby? Use 6.5 °C per 1,000 m.
steps: 2,000 m is 2 thousand meters.
2 × 6.5 = 13 °C cooler.

blocks.title: Coast or inland?
blocks.q: Two cities are at the same latitude. One is on the coast, the other far inland. Which has colder winters?
steps: The ocean warms coasts in winter.
Inland, nothing holds the heat.

blocks.html: Thinking climate depends only on latitude. Quito sits almost on the equator but averages only about 14 °C, because it is 2,850 m high. London and Calgary, Canada, are at similar latitudes, but London's winters are far milder thanks to the ocean and the North Atlantic Current. Try it in the Climate Factors lab, linked on this page.

blocks.html: With the climate controls in mind, geographers sort the world's climates into a few big groups. The system most use was first worked out by the climate scientist Wladimir Köppen in 1884 and improved over many years.
The five main climate groups are tropical (A), dry (B), temperate (C), continental (D) and polar (E). Many maps add highland climates for high mountains, where the climate changes with height.

Near 30° N and S, and deep inside continents
Mild winters, warm or hot summers
Mid-latitudes, often near coasts: southeastern U.S., western Europe
Inside large northern continents: Canada, Russia
Cold all year; even the warmest month below 10 °C
blocks.cap: The Köppen groups.

blocks.name: gg-climate
blocks.cap: A tropical rainforest climate (A) and a hot desert climate (B).

blocks.html: Each group comes from a mix of the controls. Tropical climates sit where the Sun is high all year. Dry climates form where air sinks (near 30°), behind mountains, or far from the sea. Temperate and continental climates are both in the middle latitudes; the ocean is what makes the difference: coasts get mild winters, inland areas cold ones. Group D is found almost only in the Northern Hemisphere, because the Southern Hemisphere has no large land areas at those latitudes.

blocks.title: Which group?
blocks.q: A place has a coldest month of −15 °C and a warmest month of 20 °C, with rain or snow in every season. Which group?
steps: The warmest month is above 10 °C, so it is not polar.
The coldest month is well below 0 °C, so it is not temperate.
It is wet enough not to be dry.

blocks.html: Thinking climate zones are neat bands by latitude. The bands are bent: deserts sit near 30° N and S, west coasts in the middle latitudes are milder than east coasts, and mountains have their own climates. Spain and the Sahara are close together but have different climates. Try it in the Climate Zones lab, linked on this page.

blocks.cap: Deserts cluster near the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

blocks.html: A climograph puts a whole year of climate in one picture. You can read it with the skills from scaled graphs. It shows a place's average temperature and precipitation for each month.

On a climograph, the line is the average temperature (read it on the left axis) and the bars are the precipitation (read them on the right axis). The shape tells the climate, and the warm months tell the hemisphere.

blocks.name: gg-climate
blocks.cap: A Mediterranean climate: a warm, dry summer and a mild, wet winter.

blocks.html: Two kinds of data with different units share one graph, so each needs its own scale. Putting them together shows how they line up: in a Mediterranean climate, the tallest bars come in the cool months and almost none in the hot months, which tells you summer is the dry season. In the Northern Hemisphere, July is near the warmest; in the Southern Hemisphere, it is near the coldest.

blocks.title: Reading the graph
blocks.q: On the climograph above, which months get the most rain, and is it warm or cool then?
steps: Find the tallest bars: December and January, with November and February close behind.
Look at the line in those months: the lowest temperatures of the year, about 10 to 14 °C.
blocks.a: The cool winter months are the wettest.

blocks.title: Which hemisphere?
blocks.q: A climograph shows the warmest months in December, January and February. Where is the place?
steps: Summer comes when the Sun is high.
December to February is summer only south of the equator.

blocks.name: gg-climate

titles: A marine west coast climate in the Southern Hemisphere

blocks.cap: The same kind of climate as western Europe, but in the Southern Hemisphere, as in New Zealand: the warmest months are at the start and end of the graph (December to February).

blocks.html: Reading the bars against the temperature scale (or the line against the rain scale). Before you read a value, put your finger on the right axis: °C on the left for the line, mm on the right for the bars. Also, a summer peak in July means the Northern Hemisphere; a peak in January means the Southern.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: Climate decides what can grow. Where the climate is alike, similar plants grow, and similar animals live among them, even on different continents.

A biome is a large region with a similar climate, plants and animals. The main land biomes: tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, temperate grassland, temperate forest, Mediterranean shrubland, taiga (boreal forest) and tundra.

blocks.name: gg-biome
blocks.cap: Eight biomes, with their climate, plants and animals.

head: Biome
Where
Plants
rows: Sahara, Arabia, Australia, the U.S. Southwest
Great Plains, the Pampas, the steppes of Eurasia
Eastern U.S., western Europe, eastern China
Trees that drop leaves in fall
Around the Mediterranean, California, central Chile
Mosses, lichens, low shrubs; no trees
blocks.cap: Where the biomes are.

blocks.html: Plants are fixed in place, so they must survive the local climate all year. Broad thin leaves lose water fast, so they work where it is wet; needles survive cold and dry winters; cactuses store water; grasses regrow quickly after drought or fire. The same problems get similar solutions: deserts in Africa and the Americas both have spiny, water-storing plants, even though the plants are not related.

blocks.title: Name the biome
blocks.q: A region has long, very cold winters, short summers, and forests of spruce and fir with moose and wolves. Which biome?
steps: Conifer forests in a cold climate are taiga.

blocks.html: Thinking a biome is a country, or the home of one animal. A biome is defined by climate and plants, and one biome can stretch across many countries and continents: the taiga runs from Alaska across Canada and from Norway across Russia. One country, such as Brazil or the United States, can hold several biomes.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: You can read a climograph and you know the biomes. Now connect them: two numbers, yearly temperature and yearly precipitation, predict most biomes.
Temperature and rainfall together decide the biome: hot and wet makes rainforest; hot with a long dry season, savanna; hot or cold and very dry, desert; cold with some rain, taiga; very cold, tundra.

blocks.name: gg-biome
blocks.cap: The biome chart: yearly average temperature up the side, yearly precipitation across. Tap to move the point and see which biome it lands in.

blocks.html: Warmth sets how long plants can grow; water sets how big they can get. Trees need plenty of water: with less, grasses replace them, and with even less, only desert plants survive. Cold shortens the growing season until only conifers, then only mosses and low shrubs, can live. The chart is simplified, after the ecologist Robert Whittaker (1975); real boundaries also depend on soil, fire and when in the year the rain falls.

blocks.title: Hot and dry
blocks.q: A place averages 24 °C and gets 15 cm of rain a year. Which biome?
steps: 24 °C is hot.
15 cm is very little rain, under 25 cm.

blocks.title: From a climograph
blocks.q: A climograph shows 26 to 31 °C all year, with heavy rain in half the year and almost none in the other half. Which biome?
steps: Hot all year: tropical.
A long dry season means trees are scattered and grass covers the ground.

blocks.name: gg-climate
blocks.cap: A savanna climate (A) and a taiga climate (B).

blocks.html: Matching by temperature alone. A hot place with little rain is a desert, not a rainforest; a cold place with some rain can grow taiga, while a colder, drier one is tundra. Always read both: the line and the bars.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards (NCSS, 2013), Geography, Dimension 2, grades 6-8

blocks.html: How many countries are there? It sounds like a simple question, but the answer depends on who is counting. Let us look at the most common answer and at why other lists differ. This builds on The Continents Compared.
The United Nations has 193 member states. Two more, the Holy See (Vatican City) and the State of Palestine, are UN observer states. This course uses those 195 as its list of countries.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Tap any place to read its name, its capital and whether it is a UN member, an observer state or another kind of area. Hatched areas are disputed.

blocks.html: There is no world office that decides what counts as a country. Each government decides which others it recognizes, and the UN admits new members only with the approval of its Security Council and General Assembly. So a place can govern itself, with its own leaders, money and passports, and still not be a UN member if some countries do not recognize it. The newest UN member, South Sudan, joined in 2011.

rows: Governed by the Republic of China from Taipei. The People's Republic of China claims it. Not a UN member; a small number of countries recognize it, and many others keep unofficial ties.

blocks.title: Counting
blocks.q: This course lists 193 UN members and 2 observer states. How many is that?

blocks.title: Largest and smallest
blocks.q: Which UN-listed country is the largest by area, and which is the smallest?
steps: Russia covers about 17 million km², the most of any country.
The Holy See (Vatican City) covers less than half a square kilometer, inside the city of Rome.
blocks.a: Largest: Russia. Smallest: the Holy See (Vatican City).

blocks.html: Expecting one exact count that everyone agrees on. Other lists say 196, 197 or more, because they add places that some countries recognize and others do not. When you see a count, ask: whose list is it? On this site we say "193 UN members plus 2 observer states."

blocks.html: Of the 195 countries on our list, some have no coast at all. Getting goods in and out of them means crossing a neighbor.
A landlocked country has no coast on the open ocean. There are 44 on our list: 16 in Africa, 14 in Europe, 12 in Asia and 2 in South America (Bolivia and Paraguay). Kazakhstan is the largest.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The 44 landlocked countries, highlighted. Small ones have dots.

blocks.html: A coast lets a country trade by ship, the cheapest way to move heavy goods across the world. A landlocked country must send its goods by road, rail or river through other countries to reach a port, so trade usually costs more. Many landlocked countries sign agreements with neighbors for the use of their ports. The Caspian Sea does not count as a coast: it is a lake, and no ship can sail from it to the ocean.

blocks.title: Landlocked or not?
blocks.q: Kazakhstan has a long shore on the Caspian Sea. Is it landlocked?
steps: The Caspian Sea is a lake: land surrounds it.
No route by sea leads from it to the open ocean.
blocks.a: Yes. Kazakhstan is landlocked, and it is the largest landlocked country.

blocks.title: Doubly landlocked
blocks.q: Liechtenstein is surrounded by Switzerland and Austria. Uzbekistan is surrounded by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan. What is special about them?
steps: Every neighbor of each one is also landlocked.
To reach the sea, you must cross at least two countries.
blocks.a: They are the world's only two doubly landlocked countries.

blocks.html: Counting a country on an inland sea, such as the Caspian, as coastal. Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan all touch the Caspian, and all three are landlocked. Another mix-up: Uruguay and Paraguay. Uruguay has an Atlantic coast; Paraguay is landlocked.

sources.name: CIA World Factbook, Geography sections of the country pages (cia.gov)

blocks.html: In How Many Countries? you saw that the world has 193 UN member states. Now we visit them region by region, starting close to home. (Younger learners met Canada and Mexico in Our Neighbors: Canada and Mexico.) North America runs from the Arctic down to Panama, where it meets South America.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: North and Central America: Canada, the United States, Mexico and the seven countries of Central America.

blocks.html: North America has three large countries, Canada, the United States and Mexico, and the seven small countries of Central America: Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama.

Central America is the narrow strip of land, an isthmus, that links North America to South America. It is part of the continent of North America, not a separate continent. Geographers draw its northern edge at the southern border of Mexico, so Mexico counts as North America but not as Central America.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Central America begins at Mexico's southern border. Going southeast: Guatemala and Belize, Honduras and El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama.

blocks.title: Reading the isthmus from north to south
blocks.q: Which Central American country is farthest southeast?
steps: Start at Mexico's southern border: Guatemala and Belize.
Next come Honduras and El Salvador, then Nicaragua and Costa Rica.
The last one, touching Colombia in South America, is Panama.

blocks.title: One coast or two?
blocks.q: Which Central American country has no Caribbean coast?
steps: Most Central American countries touch both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.
Belize touches only the Caribbean.
El Salvador is the one with only a Pacific coast.

blocks.html: Many people think Mexico is in Central America, or even in South America. Mexico is in North America. Central America begins at Mexico's southern border, with Guatemala and Belize. A quick check: Mexico borders the United States, and no Central American country does.

blocks.html: You can find the ten countries of North and Central America. Now let us add their capitals. A capital is the city where a country's government meets. It is often, but not always, the biggest city.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The capitals of North and Central America (stars).

head: Country
Capital
blocks.cap: Countries and capitals of North and Central America.

blocks.html: Learn the three big ones first: Ottawa (Canada), Washington, D.C. (United States) and Mexico City (Mexico). Three Central American capitals almost share their country's name: Guatemala City, San Salvador (El Salvador) and Panama City.

Countries choose capitals for many reasons, not for size. Ottawa was picked in the 1850s partly because it sat between the English-speaking and French-speaking parts of the country. Belize moved its capital inland to Belmopan in 1970, after a hurricane badly damaged Belize City on the coast.

blocks.title: A name that helps
blocks.q: What is the capital of Panama?
steps: Panama's capital has the country's name in it.
It is Panama City, on the Pacific side of the Panama Canal.

blocks.title: Biggest city or capital?
blocks.q: Is Toronto the capital of Canada?
steps: Toronto is Canada's largest city.
But the government meets in Ottawa, on the Ottawa River.

blocks.html: People often say Toronto for Canada or New York for the United States, because those are the famous big cities. The capitals are Ottawa and Washington, D.C. A good habit: when a capital comes to mind fast, ask "Is that the capital, or just the biggest city?"

blocks.html: East of Central America lies the Caribbean Sea, ringed by islands. In Islands and Peninsulas you met islands of every size; here they are countries. Thirteen island countries are UN members, and many other islands belong to countries far away.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Caribbean. Small island countries are shown with dots.

blocks.html: The big islands in the north are the Greater Antilles: Cuba, Jamaica, and Hispaniola, which Haiti (west) and the Dominican Republic (east) share. The Bahamas lie north of Cuba. The small islands curving south toward Venezuela are the Lesser Antilles, from Antigua and Barbuda down to Trinidad and Tobago.

Not every island is a country. Some islands chose independence; others stayed linked to the United States, the United Kingdom, France or the Netherlands. Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands are U.S. territories, Aruba and Curaçao are parts of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and Guadeloupe and Martinique are parts of France. So the map of the Caribbean has more islands than countries.

blocks.title: One island, two countries
blocks.q: Which two countries share Hispaniola, and which is on the west?
steps: Hispaniola is the island between Cuba and Puerto Rico.
Haiti covers the western third.
The Dominican Republic covers the eastern two-thirds.

blocks.title: Country or territory?
blocks.q: Is Puerto Rico one of the Caribbean's thirteen countries?
steps: Puerto Rico is a territory of the United States.
Its people are U.S. citizens.
So it is not an independent country.

blocks.html: It is easy to think every Caribbean island is a country. Check before you count: Puerto Rico, Aruba, Curaçao, the Cayman Islands and others belong to larger countries. Also watch two look-alike names: Dominica is a small island in the Lesser Antilles; the Dominican Republic is on Hispaniola.

blocks.cap: Your turn: find the thirteen island countries. Small ones have dots you can tap.

blocks.html: Now that you can find the Caribbean countries, add their capitals. Most are port cities, because island countries grew up around their harbors.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Caribbean capitals (stars).

head: Country
Capital
blocks.cap: Countries and capitals of the Caribbean.

blocks.html: Start with the big islands: Havana (Cuba), Kingston (Jamaica), Port-au-Prince (Haiti), Santo Domingo (Dominican Republic) and Nassau (Bahamas). Then learn the small islands in pairs from north to south.

Many capitals in the Lesser Antilles carry the names of saints or of English kings and towns: St. John's, Basseterre, Roseau, Castries, Kingstown, St. George's, Bridgetown. These names come from the colonial era, when European ships built harbors on these islands. Linking each name to its island, in order down the chain, is easier than learning them as a loose list.

blocks.title: Hispaniola's two capitals
blocks.q: Which capital is in Haiti, and which is in the Dominican Republic?
steps: Haiti is the western part of Hispaniola; its capital is Port-au-Prince, on a wide bay.
The Dominican Republic is the eastern part; its capital is Santo Domingo, on the south coast.

blocks.title: Two Kings
blocks.q: Kingston or Kingstown: which is Jamaica's capital?
steps: Kingston is Jamaica's capital.
Kingstown, with a "t", is the capital of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

blocks.html: The most common swap is on Hispaniola: putting Port-au-Prince in the Dominican Republic. Remember: Haiti is the west, and Port-au-Prince faces west into its bay. The Dominican Republic is the east, with Santo Domingo.

blocks.html: South America hangs below Central America, joined to it at Panama. It has twelve countries. One area on its north coast, French Guiana, is part of France, not a country. (See How Many Countries? for how countries are counted.)

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The twelve countries of South America.

blocks.html: Brazil is the giant: it covers almost half the continent and borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador. The Andes countries run down the west side (Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile), and Argentina fills most of the south. Two countries are landlocked: Bolivia and Paraguay.

Brazil touches so many countries because it is so large and sits in the middle of the continent's eastern half. Chile and Ecuador are both pressed against the Pacific by the Andes, with Peru or Argentina between them and Brazil. That is why they are the two that miss Brazil.

blocks.title: Uruguay or Paraguay?
blocks.q: Which one has a coast?
steps: Uruguay sits on the Atlantic coast, between Brazil and Argentina.
Paraguay is inland, north of Argentina, between Bolivia and Brazil.
blocks.a: Uruguay has the coast; Paraguay is landlocked.

blocks.title: Counting Brazil's neighbors
blocks.q: Name the South American countries that do not border Brazil.
steps: Go around Brazil: Uruguay, Argentina, Paraguay, Bolivia, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, and French Guiana (part of France).
Which of the twelve countries are missing? Chile and Ecuador.

blocks.html: Uruguay and Paraguay are the classic mix-up: both names end in "-guay", and both are small. Tie each to a picture: Uruguay is on the coast, like a harbor between two giants. Paraguay is landlocked in the middle, north of Argentina.

blocks.name: gg-outline
blocks.cap: Shapes help: long, thin Chile; small Uruguay on the coast; Paraguay with no coast; huge Brazil.

blocks.html: Here are the capitals of the twelve countries of South America. Several of them sit high in the Andes, and two famous ones are not the countries' largest cities.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The capitals of South America.

head: Country
Capital
blocks.cap: Countries and capitals of South America.

blocks.html: The capital of Brazil is Brasília, not Rio de Janeiro or São Paulo. Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre, the constitutional capital, and La Paz, the seat of government; both count.

Brasília is a planned city. Brazil's capital used to be Rio de Janeiro on the coast. In the 1950s the government built a new capital from scratch on the high plains of the interior, to draw people and roads inland, and moved there in 1960. Planned capitals appear elsewhere too: Canberra in Australia and Abuja in Nigeria, which you will meet later.

blocks.title: Capitals in the mountains
blocks.q: Which South American capitals are high in the Andes?
steps: Look along the Andes: Bogotá (Colombia), Quito (Ecuador) and La Paz (Bolivia) are all high up.
Lima (Peru) and Santiago (Chile) are lower, near the Pacific side of the mountains.

blocks.title: Biggest city or capital?
blocks.q: Guayaquil is Ecuador's largest city. Is it the capital?
steps: Guayaquil is a big port on the Pacific.
The capital is Quito, high in the Andes.

blocks.html: People often answer Rio de Janeiro or São Paulo for Brazil. Rio was the capital until 1960, and São Paulo is the largest city, but the capital is Brasília. For Bolivia, either Sucre or La Paz is right.

blocks.html: Now look past the borders at the land itself. In Mountains of the World you saw the great ranges of the world. North and South America share one big pattern: tall, young mountains in the west, wide plains in the middle, and older, lower land in the east.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The main physical features of the Americas.

blocks.html: The Rocky Mountains and the Andes run down the western side of the Americas. The Great Plains (North America) and the Pampas (South America) lie in the middle. The Amazon River drains the largest rainforest on Earth, and the Mississippi drains the middle of the United States.

The Andes rise where an ocean plate slides under South America, so they are young, high and still rising, with volcanoes and earthquakes. (Earth & Space explains the plates.) The Rockies, too, are far younger and higher than the Appalachians in the east, which are very old and worn down. Rain falling on the high west drains east across the plains, which is why the longest rivers, the Amazon and the Mississippi system, flow toward the Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico (the U.S. federal government has called it the Gulf of America since 2025).

blocks.title: Highest in the Americas
blocks.q: Where is the highest mountain in the Americas?
steps: The highest peaks are in the Andes.
Aconcagua, in Argentina near the border with Chile, is about 6,961 m (22,800 feet) high.
blocks.a: Aconcagua, in the Andes of Argentina.

blocks.title: Which way does the Amazon flow?
blocks.q: The Amazon begins in the Andes of Peru, near the Pacific. Which ocean does it reach?
steps: The Andes block the way west.
The river flows east across the whole continent.
It reaches the Atlantic Ocean in Brazil.

blocks.html: Many people think the Amazon rainforest is only in Brazil. Brazil holds about 60 percent of it. The rest spreads into Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Bolivia, Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana.

blocks.cap: Explore South America's land: tap a country to learn about it.

blocks.html: Europe is a small continent packed with countries, so we split it into four regions, as the UN does. (The count of countries comes from How Many Countries?.) Northern Europe has ten: the British Isles, the Nordic countries and the three Baltic states.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The ten countries of Northern Europe.

blocks.html: Three groups: the British Isles (the United Kingdom and Ireland), the Nordic countries (Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark) and the Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania).

Groups make a long list easy. The British Isles are two big islands in the Atlantic. Norway and Sweden share the Scandinavian Peninsula, Finland lies east of Sweden, Denmark is a small peninsula and islands north of Germany, and Iceland sits far out in the North Atlantic. The Baltic states line the east shore of the Baltic Sea.

blocks.title: The Baltic states in order
blocks.q: Name the Baltic states from north to south.
steps: Estonia is the northernmost, across the sea from Finland.
Latvia is in the middle.
Lithuania is the southernmost, next to Poland and Belarus.
From north to south they also go in alphabetical order: E, La, Li.

blocks.title: Two countries on one island
blocks.q: Which country does the island of Ireland hold besides Ireland?
steps: Most of the island is the country of Ireland.
The northeast corner, Northern Ireland, is part of the United Kingdom.

blocks.html: The three Baltic states are easy to mix up. Use the alphabet: from north to south, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania. Also, Greenland is not a country of its own: it is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark.

blocks.html: Each country of Northern Europe has its capital on or near the sea. That makes them easy to place on a map: look along the coasts.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The capitals of Northern Europe.

head: Country
Capital
blocks.cap: Countries and capitals of Northern Europe.

blocks.html: The four Nordic capitals on the mainland: Oslo (Norway), Stockholm (Sweden), Helsinki (Finland) and Copenhagen (Denmark). Plus Reykjavík (Iceland), Dublin (Ireland), London (United Kingdom), and the Baltic capitals Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius.

These capitals grew up as ports and trading towns. Oslo sits at the head of a long fjord, Stockholm on islands where a lake meets the Baltic, Helsinki on the Gulf of Finland, and Copenhagen on the narrow strait between Denmark and Sweden. Picturing the water around each one helps you keep them apart.

blocks.title: Matching the Nordic capitals
blocks.q: Which Nordic capital is farthest east?
steps: Oslo is in southern Norway, the west.
Stockholm is on Sweden's east coast.
Helsinki is across the Baltic, in Finland, farther east still.

blocks.title: The Baltic capitals
blocks.q: Riga is the capital of which Baltic state?
steps: Tallinn is Estonia's capital, Riga is Latvia's, and Vilnius is Lithuania's.

blocks.html: People swap the Nordic capitals. Pair each with a first letter clue you make up, or with its sea: Oslo, Norway (a fjord on the west side); Stockholm, Sweden; Helsinki, Finland; Copenhagen, Denmark. Then check: Oslo and Stockholm are on the same peninsula; Helsinki is across the sea.

blocks.html: Western Europe has nine countries: two large ones, France and Germany, and several smaller ones around them, including two of the world's tiniest. Five of them are landlocked, which you studied in Landlocked Countries.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The nine countries of Western Europe. Monaco and Liechtenstein are so small they appear as dots.

blocks.html: France and Germany are the big two. The Low Countries (the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg) lie between them and the North Sea. Switzerland, Austria and tiny Liechtenstein are in the Alps, and Monaco is a city-state on the Mediterranean coast.

The Low Countries are called that because much of the land is low and flat; parts of the Netherlands are below sea level, protected by dikes. The Alpine countries have no coast: the mountains wall them off from the sea. Monaco and Liechtenstein survived as tiny states because of old agreements between ruling families and their larger neighbors.

blocks.title: The Low Countries, north to south
blocks.q: Put the Low Countries in order from north to south.
steps: The Netherlands is on the North Sea, farthest north.
Belgium is in the middle, also on the coast.
Luxembourg is the small landlocked one to the south.

blocks.title: Germany's neighbors
blocks.q: How many countries border Germany?
steps: Go around it: Denmark, Poland, Czechia, Austria, Switzerland, France, Luxembourg, Belgium, the Netherlands.

blocks.html: Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg are easy to mix up. Remember the order from the sea inland: the Netherlands is the northern one on the North Sea, Belgium is below it, and Luxembourg is the small landlocked one to the south.
