blocks.html: Here are the capitals of Western Europe. Two of them share their country's name, and two countries have a twist about where the government sits.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The capitals of Western Europe.

head: Country
Capital
blocks.cap: Countries and capitals of Western Europe.

blocks.html: Paris (France), Berlin (Germany), Brussels (Belgium), Amsterdam (the Netherlands), Vienna (Austria), Bern (Switzerland) and Vaduz (Liechtenstein). Luxembourg and Monaco have capitals with the same name as the country.

A country's capital is set by its own laws, and they do not all work the same way. The Netherlands' constitution names Amsterdam as the capital, but the government and parliament meet in The Hague. Switzerland's laws name no capital at all; Bern is the "federal city", where the government sits, so it is the answer for Switzerland.

blocks.title: Switzerland's capital
blocks.q: Zurich and Geneva are famous Swiss cities. Which city is the capital?
steps: Zurich is the largest city, and Geneva hosts many international groups.
The government and parliament sit in Bern.

blocks.title: A capital with the country's name
blocks.q: What is the capital of Luxembourg?
steps: Luxembourg's capital is also called Luxembourg (sometimes Luxembourg City).

blocks.html: Two more to place by water: Vienna lies on the Danube, at the eastern edge of the Alps, and Brussels, in the middle of Belgium, is also home to the main offices of the European Union. Monaco's capital is the whole city-state, and Liechtenstein's, Vaduz, is a small town on the Rhine.
People answer Geneva or Zurich for Switzerland; the answer is Bern. For the Netherlands, Amsterdam is the capital; The Hague is where the government works, and both are accepted here.

blocks.html: Southern Europe lies along the Mediterranean Sea, on three peninsulas you met in Islands and Peninsulas: the Iberian, the Italian and the Balkan. It has fifteen countries, from large Spain and Italy to the tiny Holy See.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The countries of Southern Europe. Small ones appear as dots; hatching marks Kosovo, whose status is disputed.

blocks.html: The Iberian Peninsula holds Spain, Portugal and tiny Andorra. The Italian Peninsula holds Italy and, inside it, San Marino and the Holy See (Vatican City); Malta is an island to the south. The Balkan Peninsula holds Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania and Greece.

Six of the Balkan countries (Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and North Macedonia) were once parts of one country, Yugoslavia, which broke apart in the 1990s and 2000s. That is why there are so many small countries in one corner of the map. Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008; more than 100 UN members recognize it and many others, including Serbia, do not. It is not a UN member, so it is not counted among the fifteen.

blocks.title: Along the Adriatic
blocks.q: Going down the east coast of the Adriatic Sea from Italy, which countries do you pass?
steps: Slovenia has a short coast at the top.
Then the long coast of Croatia, with a tiny piece of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Then Montenegro, then Albania.
blocks.a: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Albania.

blocks.title: Countries inside Italy
blocks.q: Which two countries are completely surrounded by Italy?
steps: San Marino is a tiny country in north-central Italy.
The Holy See's territory, Vatican City, is inside Rome.
blocks.a: San Marino and the Holy See (Vatican City).

blocks.html: The small countries that came from Yugoslavia are easy to lose. Go from northwest to southeast: Slovenia (next to Italy and Austria), Croatia (the crescent along the coast), Bosnia and Herzegovina (inside the crescent), Serbia (inland, east), Montenegro (small, on the coast), North Macedonia (inland, north of Greece).

blocks.cap: The capitals of Southern Europe.

blocks.html: The big ones: Lisbon (Portugal), Madrid (Spain), Rome (Italy) and Athens (Greece). The Balkan capitals: Ljubljana (Slovenia), Zagreb (Croatia), Sarajevo (Bosnia and Herzegovina), Belgrade (Serbia), Podgorica (Montenegro), Skopje (North Macedonia) and Tirana (Albania).

Madrid was chosen in the 1500s partly because it sits near the middle of Spain. Most other capitals here grew where rivers and coasts made trade easy: Lisbon on the Tagus, Belgrade where the Sava meets the Danube, Rome on the Tiber. Linking a capital to its river or coast helps you place it.

blocks.title: Two that sound alike
blocks.q: Ljubljana or Zagreb: which is Slovenia's capital?
steps: Slovenia and Croatia are neighbors.
Ljubljana is the capital of Slovenia.
Zagreb is the capital of Croatia.

blocks.title: Spain's capital
blocks.q: Barcelona is Spain's second-largest city. What is the capital?
steps: Madrid, near the center of the country, is the capital.

blocks.html: The tiny states have tiny capitals. The Holy See's capital is Vatican City itself, inside Rome. San Marino's is the City of San Marino, on a mountaintop. Malta's is Valletta, a walled port. Andorra's, Andorra la Vella, high in the Pyrenees, is often called the highest capital city in Europe.

The Balkan capitals get mixed up: Ljubljana (Slovenia), Zagreb (Croatia), Sarajevo (Bosnia and Herzegovina), Skopje (North Macedonia). Learn them with the countries' order from northwest to southeast, and say each pair aloud.

blocks.html: Eastern Europe, as the UN groups it, has ten countries, from Poland and Czechia in the middle of Europe to Russia, the largest country on Earth. Several are landlocked, a word from Landlocked Countries.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The ten countries of Eastern Europe. Russia continues east across Asia. Hatching marks areas whose status is disputed.

blocks.html: In the west: Poland, Czechia (the Czech Republic), Slovakia and Hungary. To the southeast: Romania, Bulgaria and Moldova. To the east: Belarus, Ukraine and Russia, which stretches across Europe and northern Asia.

Russia counts as a European country because its capital and most of its people are west of the Ural Mountains, in Europe, even though most of its land is in Asia. Czechia and Slovakia were one country, Czechoslovakia, until they split peacefully in 1993, which is why they share a long border.

blocks.title: Slovakia or Slovenia?
blocks.q: Which one borders Czechia?
steps: Slovakia is in Central Europe, east of Czechia and north of Hungary.
Slovenia is far to the southwest, on the Adriatic next to Italy.

blocks.title: The Black Sea coast
blocks.q: Which countries of Eastern Europe have a coast on the Black Sea?
steps: Go around the sea: Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine and Russia.
Moldova comes close but has no coast.

blocks.html: Slovakia and Slovenia have almost the same name. Slovakia is next to Czechia (they were once one country); Slovenia is on the Adriatic, next to Italy and Croatia. A trick: Slovakia has a "k", like the Czech Republic's neighbor.

blocks.cap: The capitals of Eastern Europe (Moscow is to the east).

blocks.html: Warsaw (Poland), Prague (Czechia), Bratislava (Slovakia), Budapest (Hungary), Bucharest (Romania), Sofia (Bulgaria), Chișinău (Moldova), Kyiv (Ukraine), Minsk (Belarus) and Moscow (Russia).

Rivers made these cities. Budapest is two old towns, Buda and Pest, facing each other across the Danube. Bratislava is on the Danube too, and Kyiv is on the Dnieper. Knowing the river can help you find the city.

blocks.title: Budapest or Bucharest?
blocks.q: Which is the capital of Hungary?
steps: Budapest is on the Danube in Hungary.
Bucharest is the capital of Romania, to the southeast.

blocks.title: A spelling note
blocks.q: How is Ukraine's capital spelled?
steps: The Ukrainian spelling is Kyiv; older English books use Kiev.
Both are accepted here, but Kyiv is the usual English spelling today.

blocks.html: More river capitals: Warsaw is on the Vistula, Poland's longest river, and Prague is on the Vltava. Moscow, Russia's capital, is in the European part of the country, far west of the Ural Mountains. Moldova's capital, Chișinău, is often written Chisinau without the accent marks; both spellings are accepted.

blocks.title: Prague or Bratislava?
blocks.q: Czechia and Slovakia were once one country. Which capital belongs to each?
steps: Prague, on the Vltava, is the capital of Czechia.
Bratislava, on the Danube near Austria and Hungary, is the capital of Slovakia.

blocks.html: Budapest (Hungary) and Bucharest (Romania) both start with "Bu". Link the letters: Budapest has the Danube running through it; Bucharest is in Romania, farther east.

blocks.html: Europe is really a huge peninsula on the west end of Asia, with smaller peninsulas sticking out of it. You met the world's ranges in Mountains of the World; Europe's mountains, plains and rivers explain where its cities and farms are.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Europe's main mountains, plain, rivers and peninsulas.

blocks.html: Mountains: the Alps, the Pyrenees (France and Spain), the Carpathians and, in the east, the Urals, the usual border between Europe and Asia. The North European Plain stretches from France to Russia. Rivers: the Danube flows east to the Black Sea; the Rhine flows north to the North Sea. Peninsulas: Iberian, Italian, Balkan and Scandinavian.

Much of Europe is as far north as Canada, yet its west coast has mild winters. The North Atlantic Current, which continues the warm Gulf Stream, carries warm water northeast toward Europe, and the usual westerly winds bring that mild ocean air over the land. Away from the ocean, in eastern Europe, winters are much colder.

blocks.title: Comparing latitudes
blocks.q: London is at about 51.5° N. Name a Canadian city at about the same latitude.
steps: Calgary, in Alberta, is at about 51° N.
Calgary has much colder winters than London, because London gets mild air from the Atlantic.

blocks.title: Where do the rivers go?
blocks.q: A boat sails down the Danube from Germany. Which sea does it reach?
steps: The Danube rises in Germany's Black Forest.
It flows east through ten countries.
It ends in a delta on the Black Sea, in Romania and Ukraine.

blocks.html: People think Europe should be cold because it is far north. Latitude is only one control of climate (see What Controls Climate). Warm ocean water and westerly winds make western Europe much milder than places as far north in Canada or Russia.

blocks.html: Africa has 54 UN member states, more than any other continent. We start in the north, where the land faces the Mediterranean and the Sahara spreads behind it. (The count comes from How Many Countries?.)

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: North Africa with its capitals. Hatching marks Western Sahara, a disputed territory.

head: Country
Capital
blocks.cap: North Africa: countries and capitals, west to east.

blocks.html: From west to east: Morocco (capital Rabat), Algeria (Algiers), Tunisia (Tunis), Libya (Tripoli), Egypt (Cairo), and to the south, Sudan (Khartoum). Algeria is the largest country in Africa.

Almost everyone in North Africa lives near water: along the Mediterranean coast, in the Atlas Mountains' valleys, or along the Nile. Behind them lies the Sahara. That is why the capitals are on the coast or, for Cairo and Khartoum, on the Nile. Western Sahara, south of Morocco, is a disputed territory: Morocco controls most of it and claims all of it, and the Polisario Front, which proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, claims it too. The UN lists it as a non-self-governing territory, and it is not a UN member.

blocks.title: Two capitals named for their countries
blocks.q: Which North African capitals share most of their country's name?
steps: Algeria's capital is Algiers.
Tunisia's capital is Tunis.

blocks.title: Biggest city or capital?
blocks.q: Casablanca is Morocco's largest city. Is it the capital?
steps: Casablanca is the big port and business city.
The capital is Rabat, a little farther up the Atlantic coast.

blocks.html: Some people think the Sahara is a country. It is a desert that stretches across about ten countries and territories, from the Atlantic coast to the Red Sea. Algeria, Libya and Egypt all have large parts of it.

blocks.html: South of the Sahara, the bulge of Africa's west coast holds sixteen countries. Coming from North Africa, you cross the dry Sahel into greener land near the Gulf of Guinea.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The sixteen countries of West Africa. Cabo Verde is a group of islands far out in the Atlantic.

blocks.html: Three big inland countries, Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso, lie in the Sahel. Along the coast from northwest to east: Mauritania, Senegal, The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria, the most populous country in Africa. Cabo Verde is an island country out at sea.

Many West African borders were drawn by European colonial powers in the late 1800s, often along rivers or straight lines. That explains odd shapes such as The Gambia, a thin strip along the Gambia River almost surrounded by Senegal, and the narrow north-south strips of Togo and Benin.

blocks.title: Three Guineas
blocks.q: Where are Guinea, Guinea-Bissau and Equatorial Guinea?
steps: Guinea-Bissau is a small country on the west coast, south of Senegal.
Guinea is right next to it, to the southeast.
Equatorial Guinea is not in West Africa at all; it is far to the east, in Central Africa.
blocks.a: Guinea and Guinea-Bissau are neighbors in West Africa; Equatorial Guinea is in Central Africa.

blocks.title: Niger or Nigeria?
blocks.q: Which one is on the coast?
steps: Nigeria is on the Gulf of Guinea, at the east end of West Africa.
Niger is the large landlocked country north of it, in the Sahel and the Sahara.

blocks.html: Three countries share the name Guinea. Guinea and Guinea-Bissau are neighbors on the west coast. Equatorial Guinea, as its name hints, is near the equator in Central Africa. Also keep Niger (inland) and Nigeria (on the coast) apart.

blocks.html: Some to learn first: Abuja (Nigeria), Accra (Ghana), Dakar (Senegal), Bamako (Mali) and Niamey (Niger). Two have a note: Côte d'Ivoire's official capital is Yamoussoukro, while Abidjan, the biggest city, holds most offices; Benin's official capital is Porto-Novo, and the government works in Cotonou.

Nigeria moved its capital from Lagos, a crowded port in the far southwest, to Abuja, a planned city near the middle of the country, in 1991. A central capital is easier to reach from every part of a large country, and it did not belong to any one of the country's main regions.

blocks.title: Nigeria's capital
blocks.q: Is Lagos the capital of Nigeria?
steps: Lagos is Nigeria's largest city.
It was the capital until 1991.
The capital is now Abuja.

blocks.title: Neighbors with similar names
blocks.q: Conakry or Bissau: which is the capital of Guinea?
steps: Guinea's capital is Conakry.
Bissau is the capital of Guinea-Bissau, as its name says.

blocks.html: Several West African capitals are on the Atlantic coast as ports: Dakar, at the westernmost point of mainland Africa, Banjul, Bissau, Conakry, Freetown, Monrovia, Accra and Lomé. The inland capitals, Bamako and Niamey, are on the Niger River, and Ouagadougou is in the middle of Burkina Faso.
People say Lagos for Nigeria; the capital moved to Abuja in 1991. For Côte d'Ivoire, the official capital is Yamoussoukro, though Abidjan is the biggest city (both are accepted when you type).

blocks.html: Central Africa sits on the equator, in the great basin of the Congo River. Its nine countries run from Chad, on the edge of the Sahara, south to Angola. Next door, in West Africa, you met the coast of the Gulf of Guinea; it continues here.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The nine countries of Central Africa.

blocks.html: The giant is the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo), the second-largest country in Africa. Around it: the Republic of the Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Cameroon on the coast; Chad and the Central African Republic, both landlocked, to the north; Angola to the south; and the island country São Tomé and Príncipe in the Gulf of Guinea.

Two countries are named Congo because both take the name of the river. France ruled the land north and west of the river and Belgium the huge land south and east of it. When they became independent, both kept the river's name. They added "Republic" and "Democratic Republic" to tell themselves apart.

blocks.title: Which Congo?
blocks.q: Which Congo is larger, and which is its capital?
steps: The Democratic Republic of the Congo is much larger, with only a tiny piece of coast.
Its capital is Kinshasa.
The smaller Republic of the Congo has its capital at Brazzaville.

blocks.title: On the equator
blocks.q: Which countries of Central Africa does the equator cross?
steps: Follow the equator east from the Atlantic.
It crosses Gabon, the Republic of the Congo and the DR Congo.
São Tomé and Príncipe is almost exactly on it too.
blocks.a: Gabon, the Republic of the Congo and the DR Congo (and São Tomé and Príncipe).

blocks.html: The two Congos get mixed up. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (capital Kinshasa) is the large one. The Republic of the Congo (capital Brazzaville) is the smaller one, across the Congo River to the northwest.

blocks.html: Kinshasa (DR Congo), Brazzaville (Republic of the Congo), Luanda (Angola), Yaoundé (Cameroon), N'Djamena (Chad), Bangui (Central African Republic), Libreville (Gabon) and São Tomé. Equatorial Guinea has a note: in 2026 it named Ciudad de la Paz, a new city on the mainland, as its capital in place of Malabo, on Bioko Island, which still holds much of the government. Kinshasa and Brazzaville grew where the Congo River widens into a lake-like stretch called the Pool Malebo, just above a long series of rapids. Boats coming down the river had to stop there, so towns grew on both banks. Today each is the capital of a different country, and only the river separates them.

blocks.q: Which capital lies across the Congo River from Kinshasa?

blocks.q: Douala is Cameroon's biggest port. What is the capital?
steps: The capital is Yaoundé, inland.

blocks.html: East Africa, as the UN groups it, is the largest of Africa's regions: eighteen countries from the Red Sea to the Zambezi, plus islands in the Indian Ocean. Coming from North Africa, follow the Nile south into the highlands.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The eighteen countries of East Africa (the UN's Eastern Africa). Hatching marks areas whose status is disputed.

blocks.html: In the north, the Horn of Africa: Eritrea, Djibouti, Ethiopia and Somalia, with South Sudan to the west. Around Lake Victoria: Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi. Farther south: Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe and Mozambique. In the Indian Ocean: Madagascar, Comoros, Mauritius and Seychelles.

The Horn of Africa is a peninsula, not a country: the point of land that sticks out east into the Indian Ocean, shaped like a rhinoceros horn. Four countries share it. Inside Somalia, Somaliland in the north has governed itself since 1991, but Somalia and most countries consider it part of Somalia; maps show it hatched.

blocks.title: Two small neighbors
blocks.q: Rwanda and Burundi are side by side. Which is north?
steps: Rwanda is the northern one, south of Uganda.
Burundi is just south of Rwanda, on Lake Tanganyika.

blocks.title: Island countries
blocks.q: Which island country lies closest to Mozambique?
steps: Madagascar is the large island across the Mozambique Channel.
Comoros is a group of small islands at the north end of that channel.

blocks.html: Some people think the Horn of Africa is one country. It is a peninsula holding Somalia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti. Ethiopia, the largest, is landlocked: Eritrea and Djibouti lie between it and the sea.

blocks.html: Learn these first: Addis Ababa (Ethiopia), Nairobi (Kenya), Kampala (Uganda), Kigali (Rwanda), Dodoma (Tanzania), Mogadishu (Somalia), Lusaka (Zambia), Harare (Zimbabwe), Maputo (Mozambique) and Antananarivo (Madagascar).

Highland capitals such as Addis Ababa and Nairobi are high above sea level, so they are much cooler than the hot coasts at the same latitude. Two countries chose new capitals near their centers: Tanzania made Dodoma its official capital, though Dar es Salaam on the coast is the biggest city and still holds many offices; Burundi made Gitega its political capital in 2019, while Bujumbura remains its economic capital.

blocks.title: Tanzania's capital
blocks.q: Dar es Salaam is Tanzania's largest city. What is the official capital?
steps: Tanzania chose Dodoma, near the center of the country.

steps: Addis Ababa, high on the Ethiopian Highlands.

blocks.html: Southern Africa, as the UN groups it, has five countries at the southern tip of the continent, south of the Central and East African countries you have met.

blocks.cap: Southern Africa with its capitals.

blocks.html: South Africa has three capitals: Pretoria (where the president and government work), Cape Town (where parliament meets) and Bloemfontein (home of the highest court of appeal). Namibia (Windhoek) and Botswana (Gaborone) lie to the north. Lesotho (Maseru) and Eswatini (Mbabane; its royal and legislative capital is Lobamba) are small kingdoms.

South Africa split its capital three ways in 1910, when four colonies joined to form one country: each of the main parts got one branch of the government. Lesotho is an enclave: a country completely surrounded by another. It is also very high; all of its land is above 1,000 meters. Eswatini, which was called Swaziland until 2018, sits between South Africa and Mozambique.

blocks.title: Is Lesotho part of South Africa?
blocks.q: Lesotho is surrounded by South Africa on every side. Is it part of South Africa?
steps: Lesotho has its own government, king and capital, Maseru.
It is a UN member state.
blocks.a: No. It is an independent country inside South Africa.

blocks.title: Biggest city or capital?
blocks.q: Is Johannesburg one of South Africa's capitals?
steps: Johannesburg is South Africa's largest city.
The three capitals are Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.

blocks.html: Many people think Lesotho is part of South Africa, because it is completely surrounded by it. Lesotho is an independent country. Also, Johannesburg is the biggest city, but it is not one of the three capitals.

blocks.html: Africa is the second-largest continent, and its land is far more varied than many people picture. You met the world's great deserts in Deserts of the World; here they are with Africa's rivers, lakes and highlands.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Africa's main physical features.

blocks.html: The Sahara, the largest hot desert on Earth, covers the north; the Sahel is the dry grassland on its southern edge. The Nile flows north to the Mediterranean, and the Congo drains the rainforest of the middle. In the east, the Great Rift Valley holds long lakes and volcanoes, including Mount Kilimanjaro (about 5,895 m), Africa's highest peak. Lake Victoria is Africa's largest lake. The Kalahari covers much of the south.

Africa's pattern is set by the equator, which crosses its middle. Near the equator it rains most of the year, so rainforest grows in the Congo Basin. Moving north or south from there, the rain comes for only part of the year: savanna grassland. Farther still, around the tropics, dry air sinks and deserts form: the Sahara in the north, the Kalahari and Namib in the south. (See World Climate Zones.)

blocks.title: Snow near the equator
blocks.q: Kilimanjaro is only about 3 degrees south of the equator, yet it has snow and ice at the top. Why?
steps: Air gets colder as you go up, by roughly 6 °C for every 1,000 m.
Kilimanjaro rises almost 6 km above sea level.
So its top is far below freezing.

blocks.title: Which way does the Nile flow?
blocks.q: The Nile starts in East Africa. Where does it end?
steps: Its White Nile branch flows out of Lake Victoria; the Blue Nile comes from Ethiopia.
They join at Khartoum and flow north through Egypt.
The river ends in a delta on the Mediterranean Sea.

blocks.html: People often picture Africa as all desert or all jungle. It has both, and much more: wide savannas (the largest land type in Africa), high plateaus, snowy mountains such as Kilimanjaro, and huge lakes.

blocks.html: Asia is the largest continent, with more countries and people than any other. We start in its southwest, where Asia meets Europe and Africa. The UN calls this region Western Asia; it has eighteen countries, and many of them are on the Arabian Peninsula, which you met in Islands and Peninsulas.

blocks.html: In the north: Türkiye (Turkey) and the three Caucasus countries, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, plus the island of Cyprus. In the middle: Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine (a UN observer state), Jordan and Iraq. On the Arabian Peninsula: Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait.

Rivers decided where people settled here. The Tigris and Euphrates flow from the mountains of Türkiye through Syria and Iraq to the Gulf (the Persian Gulf, also called the Arabian Gulf). The land between them, Mesopotamia, was home to some of the world's first cities. The Arabian Peninsula, by contrast, is mostly desert, so its people live along the coasts and at oases.

steps: Iraq is the smaller, western country, where the Tigris and Euphrates flow.

blocks.html: East of Southwest Asia are two regions: the dry grasslands and mountains of Central Asia, and South Asia, the land south of the Himalayas, often called the Indian subcontinent.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Central and South Asia. Hatching marks Kashmir, whose parts are claimed by more than one country.

blocks.html: Central Asia has five countries whose names end in "-stan" (Persian for "land of"): Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. South Asia has Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and the island countries Sri Lanka and the Maldives. (The UN puts Iran and Afghanistan in South Asia.)

The five "-stans" are landlocked and far from any ocean, so they are dry: steppe grassland, deserts and high mountains. South Asia is shaped by the Himalayas, which wall it off from the rest of Asia, and by the summer monsoon, whose rains feed the great river plains of the Indus and the Ganges. Kashmir, in the north, is divided among India, Pakistan and China, and India and Pakistan each claim all of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir.

blocks.title: The five "-stans" by size
blocks.q: Put them in order from largest to smallest.
steps: Kazakhstan is by far the largest; it is the largest landlocked country in the world.
Then Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, close in size.
Then the two small mountain countries, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

blocks.title: Countries in the mountains
blocks.q: Which two small countries lie in the Himalayas between India and China?
steps: Nepal is the larger one, to the west.
Bhutan is the smaller one, to the east.

blocks.html: Southeast Asia lies south of China and east of India. It has eleven countries: some on a mainland peninsula, others on thousands of islands between the Indian and Pacific oceans.

blocks.html: On the mainland, the Indochina Peninsula: Myanmar (Burma), Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. On islands: Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei and Timor-Leste (East Timor). Malaysia is split: part on the Malay Peninsula, part on the island of Borneo. Laos is the only landlocked country.

Southeast Asia sits where plates of Earth's crust meet, part of the "Ring of Fire" around the Pacific, so it has many volcanoes and islands. Indonesia is made of more than 17,000 islands, the most of any country; the largest include Sumatra, Java, Borneo (shared) and the western half of New Guinea. The Philippines has more than 7,000 islands.

steps: The southern part is Indonesia.
The north coast is Malaysia.
Tiny Brunei sits on the north coast, surrounded by Malaysia.

steps: Cambodia lies between Thailand, Laos and Vietnam on the Indochina Peninsula.

blocks.html: Asia has the highest mountains, the highest plateau and some of the longest rivers on Earth. You met them briefly in Mountains of the World and Great Rivers of the World; here is how they fit together.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Asia's main mountains, plateaus, deserts and rivers.

blocks.html: The Himalayas, with Mount Everest (about 8,849 m), wall off South Asia. North of them is the Plateau of Tibet, the largest high plateau on Earth. Cold Siberia covers the north, and dry lands stretch from the Arabian Peninsula to the Gobi. Great rivers: the Yangtze and Yellow in China, the Ganges and Indus in South Asia, the Mekong in Southeast Asia, and the Tigris and Euphrates in the southwest.

The Plateau of Tibet averages more than 4,500 m high and holds a huge store of snow and glacier ice. Water runs off it in every direction, so many of Asia's great rivers begin on or near it: the Yangtze and Yellow flow east, the Mekong south, and the Indus and Brahmaputra west and east around the Himalayas; the Ganges begins nearby on the Himalayas' southern side. Hundreds of millions of people depend on those rivers.

blocks.title: Where do the rivers start?
blocks.q: The Yangtze reaches the sea at Shanghai. Where does it begin?
steps: Trace it upstream, west across China.
It begins high on the Plateau of Tibet.

blocks.title: A cold desert
blocks.q: Is the Gobi hot like the Sahara?
steps: The Gobi lies far north, in Mongolia and northern China, and is high up.
Its winters are bitterly cold.
It is a cold desert, mostly gravel and rock.
blocks.a: No; it is a cold desert.

blocks.html: People imagine Asia's great rivers starting in many different places. Many of them, including the Yangtze, Mekong and Indus, begin on or near the same high land: the Plateau of Tibet.

blocks.html: Oceania is the continent of Australia plus the thousands of islands of the Pacific. You compared it with other continents in The Continents Compared. It has fourteen countries: one large one, a few middle-sized ones, and many tiny island nations.

blocks.name: gg-map

blocks.html: Australia covers a whole continent. New Zealand and Papua New Guinea are next in size. The Pacific islands are grouped in three regions: Melanesia (Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji), Micronesia (Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, Nauru, Kiribati) and Polynesia (Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu). The UN groups New Zealand with Australia.

The three names come from Greek: Melanesia means "black islands", Micronesia "small islands" and Polynesia "many islands". Micronesia's islands are mostly tiny coral atolls north of the equator. Polynesia is a huge triangle with Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island at its corners. Many Pacific islands still belong to other countries, such as France's New Caledonia and French Polynesia.

blocks.html: Australia is the smallest and flattest continent, and Antarctica, at the bottom of the globe, is the coldest. You compared all seven continents in The Continents Compared.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Australia's and New Zealand's main physical features.

blocks.html: Most of Australia's interior is the dry Outback, with deserts such as the Great Victoria. The Great Dividing Range runs down the east coast, and most Australians live on the coasts, especially the southeast. The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, stretches more than 2,300 km off the northeast coast. New Zealand's Southern Alps run down the South Island. Antarctica has no countries: the Antarctic Treaty (1959) keeps it for peaceful use and science.

Antarctica is almost all ice: about 98 percent of the land is buried under an ice sheet averaging almost 2 km thick. No one lives there permanently, only scientists and staff at research stations. Seven countries had claimed parts of it; the Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959, sets those claims aside, bans military activity, and lets every member country do science anywhere on the continent.

blocks.q: Why do most Australians live near the coast?
steps: The interior, the Outback, is hot and dry.

The continent is kept for peace and science.

People live where they can grow food and find water: river valleys, plains, and warm, wet coasts. Deserts, ice sheets, high mountains and the cold far north have very few people. blocks.html: A country can have many people and still feel empty, or few people and feel crowded. To compare, we use population density: the number of people per square kilometer. It is a unit rate, like those in Unit Rates, built from a country's population and its area.
Population density = people ÷ land area. The answer is in people per square kilometer (people per km²).

Dividing shares the people out evenly: if 600 people live on 3 km², and they spread out evenly, each square kilometer has 600 ÷ 3 = 200 people. Real people are never spread evenly, so density is an average. It lets us compare a giant country and a tiny one fairly.

blocks.title: An island
blocks.q: An island has 12,000 people on 40 km² of land. What is its population density?
steps: Density = people ÷ area.

blocks.title: Many people, but less crowded
blocks.q: Bangladesh has about 174 million people on about 148,000 km². The United States has about 345 million on about 9.8 million km². Which is more crowded?
steps: Bangladesh: 174,000,000 ÷ 148,000 ≈ 1,200 people per km².
United States: 345,000,000 ÷ 9,800,000 ≈ 35 people per km².
Bangladesh has half as many people but is more than 30 times as crowded.

blocks.html: More than half the world's people live in towns and cities, and some cities hold more people than whole countries. Which city is the biggest? The answer depends on where you draw a city's edge. You will need Crowded Places to see why.

blocks.html: In the UN's 2025 count (World Urbanization Prospects), the largest cities are Jakarta, Indonesia (nearly 42 million people), Dhaka, Bangladesh (almost 40 million), and Tokyo, Japan (about 33 million). Nine of the top ten are in Asia; Cairo is the only one outside it. A megacity has 10 million people or more; there were 33 in 2025.

A city has no sharp edge: suburbs and towns run into one another. One list counts only the city's official limits; another counts the whole built-up area; another counts everyone who commutes in. The UN's 2025 report uses a new method that counts the area where people actually live close together, using maps of population density. Its older 2018 list, using countries' own city boundaries, put Tokyo first, with about 37 million.

blocks.title: Comparing two cities
blocks.q: In the UN's 2025 count, about how many more people does Jakarta have than Tokyo?
steps: Jakarta: nearly 42 million. Tokyo: about 33 million.

blocks.title: Why lists disagree
blocks.q: A book from 2019 says Tokyo is the largest city. Is the book wrong?
steps: It probably used the UN's 2018 list, which put Tokyo first.
The 2025 report measures cities differently.
blocks.a: Not wrong for its source and year; lists differ in how they draw city edges.

blocks.html: People expect one fixed ranking of cities. In the UN's older lists Tokyo was first; the 2025 report, which measures cities by where people actually live close together, puts Jakarta first. When you quote a ranking, give its source and year.
